blog.title: How to Increase FPS in PC Games Without Upgrading Your Hardware
blog.content:
Playing PC games can be frustrating when the game feels slow, the screen freezes for a moment, or movements do not look smooth. These problems often happen because of low FPS, background applications, incorrect graphics settings, or other performance issues.

The good news is that you do not always need to buy a new graphics card, processor, or gaming PC to improve your gaming experience. A few changes to your game settings, Windows configuration, and system maintenance can help your computer run games more smoothly.

In this guide, you will learn how to increase FPS in PC games without upgrading your hardware. We will cover graphics settings, driver updates, background applications, Windows optimizations, overheating, and other practical ways to improve gaming performance.

What Is FPS and Why Does It Matter in Gaming?

FPS stands for Frames Per Second. It measures how many individual images your computer displays every second while running a game.

Higher FPS generally makes gameplay look smoother, especially in fast-paced games such as first-person shooters, racing games, and competitive multiplayer titles.

Here is a simple explanation of common FPS levels:

  • 30 FPS: Playable for many games, but movement may feel less smooth.

  • 60 FPS: A common target for smooth gameplay.

  • 120 FPS: Provides smoother motion on a compatible display.

  • 144 FPS or higher: Can benefit competitive gaming when your hardware and monitor support it.

Higher FPS is not always necessary for every game. The best target depends on the type of game, your monitor's refresh rate, and your computer's capabilities.

It is also important to understand that FPS and internet lag are different problems. Low FPS usually relates to your computer's performance, while network lag is often caused by connection quality, latency, or server issues.

1. Lower Your Game's Graphics Settings

One of the easiest ways to improve FPS is to adjust the graphics settings inside the game.

Modern games include detailed shadows, reflections, lighting effects, and textures. These features can look impressive but may place a heavy load on your graphics card.

Start by lowering the settings that usually affect performance the most.

Recommended Graphics Settings

Graphics Setting Suggested Starting Point
Resolution Reduce slightly if FPS is too low
Shadows Low or Medium
Ambient Occlusion Low or Off
Reflections Low
Volumetric Effects Low
Anti-Aliasing Medium or Low
Motion Blur Off, if preferred
Texture Quality Medium or Low if video memory is limited
Ray Tracing Off if performance is poor

These are general starting points, not universal rules. The effect of each setting depends on the game and your hardware.

If you want the best settings for higher FPS, change one or two options at a time and test the results. This makes it easier to identify which settings improve performance without making the game look unnecessarily poor.

2. Reduce the Game Resolution

Resolution determines how many pixels your graphics card needs to render. Higher resolutions usually require more graphics processing power.

For example, if a game runs poorly at 1920 × 1080, try a lower supported resolution and compare the FPS.

You can also use an in-game resolution scaling option or a supported upscaling technology, such as NVIDIA DLSS, AMD FSR, or Intel XeSS, where available.

These features can render a game at a lower internal resolution and reconstruct the image to improve performance.

However, reducing resolution can make the picture less sharp. Try different settings to find a balance between image quality and smooth gameplay.

3. Close Unnecessary Background Applications

Applications running in the background can consume CPU time, RAM, storage activity, and other system resources.

Before launching a demanding game, close programs you do not need, such as:

  • Unnecessary browser tabs

  • Video-editing software

  • Large downloads

  • Unused launchers

  • Background streaming applications

  • Other resource-intensive programs

You can use Windows Task Manager to identify applications that are consuming significant resources.

Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Review the Processes tab and close only applications you recognize and do not need.

Avoid ending unfamiliar Windows processes or security software. Some background services are essential for your computer to operate correctly.

Managing background applications is a useful way to increase FPS without upgrading PC hardware, especially when your computer has limited RAM or CPU resources.

4. Update Your Graphics Card Drivers

Graphics drivers help Windows and games communicate with your graphics card. Driver updates may improve performance, fix bugs, and resolve compatibility problems in specific games.

If you are experiencing poor performance, check whether a suitable driver update is available.

How to Update Your GPU Drivers

  1. Identify your graphics card using Task Manager, Device Manager, or Windows System Information.

  2. Visit the official website of NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel, depending on your GPU.

  3. Download the appropriate driver for your graphics card and version of Windows.

  4. Follow the installation instructions.

  5. Restart your computer if requested.

  6. Launch the game and compare performance.

These GPU driver updates for gaming can be particularly helpful when a game has recently launched or received a major update.

However, a newer driver does not guarantee higher FPS in every game. If a new driver causes problems, consult the manufacturer's official guidance for troubleshooting or reverting to a stable version.

Avoid downloading drivers from unknown websites.

5. Use Windows Gaming Optimization Settings

Windows includes several features that can help improve the gaming experience. Their impact varies depending on your hardware, installed applications, and the game you play.

Enable Game Mode

Game Mode helps Windows manage certain background activities while you play.

To check it:

  1. Open Windows Settings.

  2. Select Gaming.

  3. Open Game Mode.

  4. Turn it on if it is available.

Review Startup Applications

Some applications launch automatically when Windows starts and continue running in the background.

Open Task Manager and select Startup apps. Disable unnecessary applications that you do not need to launch automatically.

Do not disable essential security or system software simply to gain FPS.

Adjust Power Settings

On a laptop, check that Windows is not using a power-saving mode that limits gaming performance.

Select an appropriate power mode in Windows Settings. Higher-performance modes may increase power consumption, heat, and fan noise.

These Windows gaming optimization tips can help reduce unnecessary resource usage without requiring new hardware.

6. Turn Off Unnecessary Overlays and Recording Features

Gaming overlays can provide useful information, but they may also consume system resources or cause compatibility issues on some computers.

Examples include:

  • Game recording features

  • Unnecessary third-party overlays

  • Background gameplay capture

  • Overlays from communication or gaming applications

If you are experiencing low FPS, temporarily disable features you do not use and test the game again.

Windows also provides recording and capture settings that may affect performance in certain situations.

Do not disable every gaming feature automatically. If an overlay is not causing problems, removing it may make little or no difference.

7. Check Your PC for Overheating

Heat can affect gaming performance. When a CPU or GPU becomes too hot, it may reduce its operating speed to protect itself. This behaviour is commonly called thermal throttling.

If your FPS starts high but drops after several minutes of gameplay, overheating may be one possible cause.

Signs of Overheating

  • FPS decreases during long gaming sessions.

  • Fans become unusually loud.

  • The computer feels excessively hot.

  • Performance improves after the system cools down.

What You Can Do

Keep the laptop or desktop in a well-ventilated area. Make sure air vents are not blocked by walls, blankets, or other objects.

Remove dust from vents and cooling areas carefully, following the manufacturer's instructions. If the system has persistent overheating problems, professional cleaning or servicing may be necessary.

Avoid placing a laptop on soft surfaces that block its air intake.

Keeping your system cool can help maintain stable performance, although it will not increase FPS beyond what your hardware and game can support.

8. Free Up Storage Space

Games may need storage space for updates, temporary files, shader caches, and other data. A nearly full drive can also make general system maintenance more difficult.

Check your available storage space and remove files you no longer need.

On Windows, you can use the built-in Storage settings or Disk Cleanup to remove suitable temporary files.

If a game is installed on a slow or problematic drive, loading times and occasional asset-streaming stutters may improve when using a faster supported drive. However, moving a game to an SSD does not automatically increase average FPS in every situation.

For most users, the first step is to maintain sufficient free storage and check for drive-related errors if problems continue.

9. Adjust Your Game's Display Mode

Some games offer several display modes, including fullscreen, borderless fullscreen, and windowed mode.

The performance difference between these modes depends on the game, Windows version, graphics driver, and system configuration.

If you are experiencing performance problems, test the available display modes and compare the results.

Also check your monitor's refresh rate in Windows display settings. If your monitor supports a higher refresh rate, make sure the correct option is selected.

Remember that a 144 Hz monitor does not automatically make a game run at 144 FPS. Your computer must still render enough frames to reach that level.

10. Use an Appropriate FPS Limit

An FPS limit restricts the maximum number of frames a game can render each second.

Although unlimited FPS may sound ideal, it can sometimes create unnecessary GPU usage, increased temperatures, and inconsistent frame delivery.

For example, if your computer can maintain approximately 60 FPS in a demanding game, setting a reasonable limit near that level may help produce more consistent performance.

A limit that is too high may not solve stuttering, while a limit that is too low can unnecessarily restrict performance.

You can test the game's built-in FPS limiter or a supported driver-level option. Use V-Sync or variable refresh rate features according to your monitor and personal preferences, as these can affect tearing, latency, and smoothness.

11. Reduce Stuttering in PC Games

Low average FPS is not the only reason a game may feel slow. Stuttering happens when individual frames take much longer to render than others, causing brief pauses or uneven movement.

A game averaging 60 FPS can still feel unpleasant if frame delivery is inconsistent.

If you want to reduce stuttering in PC games, try these steps:

  • Close unnecessary background applications.

  • Update the game and check for known performance issues.

  • Install a suitable, stable graphics driver.

  • Lower demanding graphics settings.

  • Check CPU, GPU, RAM, and storage usage during gameplay.

  • Make sure the system is not overheating.

  • Allow shader compilation to finish when the game requires it.

  • Check whether the game is installed on a drive experiencing problems.

Shader compilation can cause temporary stuttering in some games, especially after updates or when entering a new area. Repeatedly deleting shader caches is not always helpful and may cause shaders to compile again.

If stuttering occurs mainly during online matches, check your network connection as well. Network lag can look like a performance problem, but it requires different troubleshooting steps.

12. Choose the Right Settings for Low-End PCs

Older computers and entry-level gaming PCs often need more careful settings to run demanding games smoothly.

If you want to improve gaming performance on low-end PC hardware, focus on reducing unnecessary processing rather than chasing maximum visual quality.

Try the following:

Use Low or Medium graphics settings: Start with shadows, reflections, and advanced effects.

Lower resolution if needed: This can reduce GPU workload, especially when the graphics card is the limiting factor.

Close background programs: Free up RAM and CPU resources.

Avoid unnecessary recording: Background video capture can affect performance on some systems.

Check the game's minimum requirements: Some games may not run smoothly on hardware below their requirements, regardless of settings.

Use supported upscaling features: If available, these can improve performance while maintaining acceptable image quality.

You can also check whether the game has a performance mode or a recommended preset for lower-powered systems.

Not every game can be made smooth through software adjustments alone. If the CPU, GPU, or available RAM is below the game's practical requirements, improvements may be limited without a hardware change.

How to Fix Low FPS in Games: A Quick Checklist

If you are still experiencing performance problems, use this checklist to narrow down the cause.

  • Lower graphics settings and test the game.

  • Reduce resolution or enable supported upscaling.

  • Close unnecessary background applications.

  • Check for suitable graphics driver updates.

  • Enable Windows Game Mode if appropriate.

  • Check CPU and GPU temperatures.

  • Verify that the monitor is using its intended refresh rate.

  • Check whether the game is running on the intended GPU, especially on laptops with integrated and dedicated graphics.

  • Confirm that the PC meets the game's system requirements.

  • Test performance in the same game area to make comparisons more reliable.

These steps can help you identify how to fix low FPS in games without spending money immediately.

How to Get Smoother Gameplay on PC

Getting smoother gameplay is about more than achieving the highest possible FPS. Stable frame times, sensible graphics settings, good cooling, and a properly configured system all contribute to a better experience.

Start by measuring your FPS before making changes. Adjust a small number of settings, test the game again, and compare the results under similar conditions.

If your FPS improves but the game still feels uneven, look at frame-time consistency, temperature, memory usage, and background activity.

Following these steps can help you understand how to get smoother gameplay on PC while keeping your existing hardware.

Conclusion

Improving gaming performance does not always require buying new computer components. By adjusting graphics settings, managing background applications, updating drivers, optimizing Windows, and keeping your PC cool, you may be able to achieve better FPS and more consistent gameplay.

The most effective approach is to make changes gradually and test the results. Every PC and game behaves differently, so there is no single setting that works perfectly for everyone.

Start with the simplest adjustments and focus on stable performance rather than the highest possible number. With the right configuration, you can often make better use of your existing hardware and enjoy a smoother PC gaming experience.

faqs.question: Can I increase FPS without upgrading my PC?
faqs.answer: Yes, you may be able to improve FPS by lowering graphics settings, reducing resolution, closing unnecessary applications, updating graphics drivers, and resolving overheating. The results depend on your hardware and the game.

faqs.question: What settings give the highest FPS in PC games?
faqs.answer: Lowering resolution, shadows, reflections, and demanding visual effects often improves FPS. The best combination depends on the game, graphics card, and whether the CPU or GPU is limiting performance.

faqs.question: Does updating graphics drivers increase FPS?
faqs.answer: Driver updates can improve performance or fix problems in certain games, but they do not guarantee higher FPS in every situation. Download drivers from the official graphics card manufacturer's website.

faqs.question: Does Game Mode improve gaming performance?
faqs.answer: Windows Game Mode can help manage certain background activities, but its effect varies by computer and game. It is worth testing, although it may not produce a noticeable improvement on every system.

faqs.question: Why does my FPS drop after playing for some time?
faqs.answer: Possible causes include overheating, increasing system resource usage, memory limitations, background applications, and game-specific issues. Check temperatures and system usage to identify the likely cause.
